title: Going to War and Going to College: Did World War II and the G.I. Bill Increase Educational Attainment for Returning Veterans?
research_question: Did serving in the military during World War II, together with the postwar educational benefits made available to returning servicemen, raise the postsecondary educational attainment of veterans relative to what they would have attained absent service and benefits? Specifically, what was the magnitude of the combined effect on years of college completed and on college completion rates for white male veterans?
data_description: The primary data source is a 3% public-use microdata sample from the 1970 U.S. Decennial Census (an aggregation of three 1% files), supplemented by the 1960 and 1980 Decennial Census files for robustness, and the 1979 Survey of Veterans for detailed information on benefit utilization. The unit of observation is the individual white male, aggregated to year-quarter-of-birth cells for the cohort-level analysis. Key variables include year and quarter of birth, race, veteran status (including conflict served), highest grade attended, years of college completed (0–4), and college completion (16+ years of schooling). The sample focuses on white men born in the continental United States, primarily covering birth cohorts from 1923 through 1938, with extensions back to 1908 for descriptive cohort trends. Observations with allocated values for sex, age, race, quarter of birth, veteran status, or education are excluded.
institutional_context: The setting is U.S. military mobilization for World War II and the subsequent provision of educational benefits under the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944 (the G.I. Bill). The 1940 Selective Service Act required registration and conscription, and as the war progressed chronological birth date became the dominant determinant of induction probability, with over 75% of white men born between 1920 and mid-1926 serving, followed by a sharp drop in service rates for cohorts born after mid-1926 who were too young to serve before V-J Day. Returning veterans serving more than 90 days were eligible for up to four years of benefits, including up to $500 per year in tuition and books plus a monthly stipend, representing an unprecedented and broadly available federal subsidy for college. The subsequent Korean conflict drew heavily from cohorts born in the late 1920s and early 1930s, who were eligible for a somewhat less generous parallel benefit program, complicating the post-WWII counterfactual.
